land.text: Mahan, the south-west and the Han valley

successors.note: The Samhan succeeded Jin: 'Records of the Three Kingdoms say Jinhan succeeded Jin, while the Book of the Later Han says Mahan, Jinhan, and Byeonhan were all part of the former Jin state' (Jin page).

land.text: Jinhan, the south-east east of the Nakdong

successors.note: Jinhan's rulers claimed succession from Jin (Jinhan page).
The Byeonhan page: 'Byeonhan, like the other Samhan confederacies, appears to be descended from the Jin state of southern Korea'.

correction.text: the Cliopatria Jin shape without the Ye coast: Jin held 'some portion of the southern Korean peninsula', with its capital 'somewhere south of the Han River'

keyframe_review.note: -197..-111, 112,814 km2: the area of Mahan, Byeonhan, Jinhan and Dongye together (49,731 + 13,603 + 23,506 + 25,776 = 112,616 km2), so Cliopatria draws the Ye coast (Gangwon and southern Hamgyong) as Jin land. The Jin page puts Jin in the 'southern Korean peninsula' and gives no area, and the Eastern Ye page puts that coast under Wiman Joseon in 129 BCE ('It belonged to the Wiman Joseon in 129 BC'), Han from 128 BCE and Lintun from 108. The pages are silent on the coast before 129 BCE, so the cut is certain only from then. Unverified beyond that: page budget.

correction.text: the same shape without the Ye coast, held -110..-92

keyframe_review.note: -110..-92, same outline and area as the first shape (112,814 km2). The Ye coast was then Han's Lintun Commandery (108 BCE; 'it was reorganized into Lintun Commandery(108 BC)'), not Jin land. The Jin page's own infobox map is 'Jin state in 108 BCE'; its end is 'somewhat contradictory' and the infobox says the Samhan succeeded it in the 2nd century BCE, so -92 is at best late.

region.text: the Cliopatria Jin shape without the Ye coast; 'some portion of the southern Korean peninsula'

ledger.note: 197 BCE: Jin enters the map in the south of the peninsula. The page gives only 'the 4th century BCE' for its establishment, says its capital is unknown ('somewhere south of the Han River') and that King Jun 'is reported to have fled to Jin after Wiman seized his throne' (194 BCE on the Gojoseon page); -197 is Cliopatria's first shape.

92 BCE: Jin's land divides into the Samhan. 'Mahan, Jinhan, and Byeonhan' succeeded it (Jin page); Cliopatria starts the three in 91 BCE. The Samhan page says they 'formed around the time of the fall of Old Chosŏn' in 108 BCE and the Jin infobox says the 2nd century BCE, so the year is a bridge, not a page date.
92 BCE: Jinhan emerges from Jin; the Records of the Three Kingdoms say 'Jinhan succeeded Jin'.
92 BCE: Byeonhan emerges from Jin; the Book of the Later Han says Mahan, Jinhan and Byeonhan 'were all part of the former Jin state'.
92 BCE: Jin gives way to the three Han confederacies. 'Records are somewhat contradictory on Jin's demise'; no exact year is given.

certainty.note: The page gives no frontier and no capital; the Cliopatria shape is a core of the south.

sources.title: Jin (Korean state)
sources.note: Identity, 4th to 2nd centuries BCE, capital unknown, King Jun, succession by the Samhan; no area.

sources.title: Samhan
sources.note: King Jun fled to Jin 'around 194-180 BCE'; the Samhan formed around 108 BCE; Mahan, Jinhan, Byeonhan.

sources.title: Gojoseon
sources.note: King Jun fled to Jin; Jin arose 'by the 3rd century BCE' on this page against '4th century' on the Jin page.

sources.title: Wiman Joseon
sources.note: King Ugeo 'prevented the Jin state from communicating with the Han dynasty'.

sources.title: Eastern Ye
sources.note: The Ye coast under Wiman Joseon (129 BCE), Han (128 BCE), Lintun (108 BCE).

notes: Cliopatria's Korean Jin (Q1155101) is the union of the Samhan rows plus Dongye (the area of -197..-92 equals Mahan + Byeonhan + Jinhan + Dongye within 200 km2), so the shape reaches the east coast up to 39.1N; the pages do not support that for the Ye coast (Wiman Joseon, then Han, from 129 BCE) and both keyframes are adjusted to remove it; the Dongye dossier starts the Ye in 82 BCE. The state is older than its row: the Jin page gives 'the 4th century BCE' (the Gojoseon page 'by the 3rd century BCE') and no year, so found is at confidence 1 on Cliopatria's first year. The end is also a bridge: Jin page infobox, the Samhan 'succeeded' it in the 2nd century BCE; the Samhan page, they 'formed around the time of the fall of Old Chosŏn' in 108 BCE; the Mahan, Byeonhan and Jinhan infoboxes each give an establishment of 194 BCE (against 'around the beginning of the Common Era' and 'the 1st century BCE' in their own text), which coincides with the date of King Jun's flight. Cliopatria's -92/-91 is kept. King Jun (Gija Joseon) 'fled to the state of Jin ... around 194-180 BCE' (Samhan page); the Mahan page adds a Cheongju Han clan list giving Jun a reign of 220-193 BCE and a last king Gye of 33-17 BCE, which Korean historians reject with the Gija genealogy. Capital: the page lists 'Unknown'; no dot is drawn. No war: the pages say only that Wiman Joseon 'prevented direct contact between Jin and China'. Page budget: 2 pages of its own (Jin, Samhan) plus three opened for neighbours.
